entries.note: First described ships at sea, then became African-American slang and a sexual euphemism; hosts also discuss how to spell it.
Reportedly coined by Billboard magazine as a euphemism to replace the label 'race music'.
Music industry term for records marketed to African-American audiences from the 1920s to the 1940s.
Industry term for bluegrass-style music marketed to white Southern audiences; it developed into country music.
Meant sadness long before the genre; the genre name came from song titles like 'Memphis Blues'.
Dates to the 1600s, meaning harmful spirits, hallucinations and mental anguish; later used for sadness or despair.
African-American term for an informal place for music, dancing and gambling; probably from a Gullah word meaning rowdy.
Takes its name from the juke joint.
Pun on beetles and beat, inspired by Buddy Holly's Crickets; earlier they were briefly called the Silver Beatles.
Stage name of musician Brian Cassar; the hosts suggest it was borrowed from the ballad of Casey Jones.
Originally the Ravens; possibly chosen as a gimmick hinting at kinkiness, or just for subversive publicity.
An announcer forgot the band's name and used their song title instead; some broadcasters refused to say it.
Named after a dildo in William S. Burroughs' novel Naked Lunch.
Supposedly named for the average amount a man ejaculates.
From a remark that the supergroup would go down like a lead balloon; spelled 'Led' so it wouldn't be misread.

entries.term: go down like a lead balloon
entries.note: The idiom behind Led Zeppelin's name; the hosts discuss whether Americans use it.
Started as 'Deaf Leopard' in a school art lesson; respelled playfully, echoing Led Zeppelin.
Deliberately misspelled tribute to Leonard Skinner, a gym teacher at their school; pronounced 'Leonard Skinner'.
Guitar shop founded by a Lynyrd Skynyrd roadie who survived the plane crash; spelled with y's like the band's name.
Unnecessary umlauts in band names like Mötley Crüe and Motörhead, meant to look Germanic and dark.
Originally Spice; renamed after the Dickens villain in the 100th anniversary year of Dickens' death.
Taken from a passage in Virginia Woolf's story 'The Mark on the Wall'.
Originally El Grupo de Rock and Roll; renamed after a film and play whose title refers to Don Quixote.
Named after Aldous Huxley's essay The Doors of Perception, which quotes William Blake.
First suggested by a psychiatrist in a letter to Aldous Huxley about their mescaline experiments.
Named after a 1963 non-fiction exposé on non-heterosexual sex, later reclaimed by queer culture.
Named after Greenwich Village, birthplace of the modern LGBTQ rights movement; created for the gay disco market.
Named after a Boris Karloff horror film, since horror films drew paying crowds.
The hosts praise it as a strong classical reference.
Sanskrit word meaning to blow away or wipe out; release from karma and rebirth.
A genre name given by people who disliked the music.
Meant horrible or inferior; applied to the music and embraced by musicians for its rawness.
Previously Big Fat Noises and Starfish; the name came from a 1997 poetry collection.
First recorded as Darlin'; the name came from a Melody Maker review calling them 'a daft punky thrash'.
A fan's praise: 'fett' meant great and 'Brot' was slang for hash, so 'really good hash'.
Chosen because the band was very into industry.
Name of a German band meaning the doctors.
A popular German band named after an idiom about having nothing going on.
Means having nothing going on: being bored or wasting time.
From a deadly air show crash at the Ramstein US air base; the extra M was a misspelling.
The singer's name is the Icelandic word for birch.
Also the name of the lead singer's younger sister, born as the band was forming.
The Italian Eurovision winners have a Danish name, suggested by their half-Danish bassist.
Name of the duo who sang the Macarena.
Name of the band known for La Bamba.
The band says it stands for 'Beyond the Scene', but it originally abbreviates the Korean for bulletproof boy scouts.
A Taylor Swift lyric that became a meme; Jess picked it up without knowing where it came from.
Belgian singer's name is 'maestro' with its two syllables swapped, using Verlan.
French back slang that rearranges the syllables or sounds of words; a long-standing tradition.
Verlan for 'femme' (woman), used by young French people.
Verlan form of 'bizarre'.
Verlan greeting that Rob challenges Jess to work out from the most common French greeting.
Verlan for 'français'.
Verlan for 'merci'.
Title of a Renaud album; Verlan for 'laisse tomber', meaning let it go or just leave it.
